summary: Spotted knapweed is a plant up to 3 feet tall with purple, thistle-like flowers that have a spotted appearance at their base. It spreads quickly in disturbed areas and can also invade undisturbed places because it sprouts very early in spring and releases chemicals that harm other plants. Animals don't like to eat it, which reduces food for livestock and wildlife, and it has been linked to more soil erosion. Its thick taproot allows it to grow in poor, rocky, or sandy soils.
history: Spotted knapweed originally comes from southeastern Europe. It arrived in North America by accident, mixed in with contaminated seed and ships' ballast. The plant spreads mainly through its seeds.
seasons: Spotted knapweed starts out as a low rosette of leaves that are 6 to 8 inches long in its first year. In later years, it grows much taller—up to 3 feet—with flowers at the ends of many branches, and a single plant can live up to nine years. Each plant can produce up to 1,000 seeds that spread by wind.

handling.text: Several insects and fungi have been released to help control spotted knapweed, with varying success, and herbicides can reduce it. Its seeds build up in the soil and resist heat, so control takes ongoing monitoring, and burning or composting only works at very high temperatures. In New York City parks like Kissena, cutting, killing or removing plants without permission from NYC Parks is against park rules, so report it instead.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks like Kissena Park, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
